Guard0 meeting notes (Feb 11, Dallas VC call)

1) What Guard0 is building

Guard0 is positioning as an **AI security + governance platform** that sits across the enterprise’s AI stack (apps, agents, models, tools, data) and answers two urgent buyer needs:

* **“What do we have?”** Full **AI/agent inventory + asset graph** across code + cloud + agent platforms.

* **“What can go wrong?”** **Context-aware, non-deterministic security testing** (dynamic attacks) for AI apps and agents.

* **“How do we operationalize controls?”** **Governance + workflows** integrated into agent platforms and developer/AppSec tooling.

They explicitly dislike “AI AppSec = old AppSec policies relabeled for AI” and claim their core advantage is **dynamic testing driven by business context**, not deterministic policy checks.

* * *

2) Founder background (as stated)

* Founder spent ~6 years building API security / posture management (mentions acquisition; likely referencing Traceable AI experience).

* Early career includes hands-on product + GTM + customer success in an early-stage context.

* MS from Stanford University.

* Last ~8 months focused full-time on Guard0 (product came from customer discovery in 2024–2025, especially regulated enterprises).

* * *

3) Product pillars (how they describe it)

Pillar A: AI + Agent discovery (inventory)

Goal: give CISOs/CSOs visibility without slowing engineering.

* Data sources: “code + cloud sync” (implies deep integration into CI/CD + cloud control plane + logs; they explicitly mention visibility across Microsoft Azure / Google Cloud / AWS signals).

* Output: “95%+ AI landscape” view: AI apps, models, prompts, tool access, DB access, MCPs, agent platform usage, and activity.

**Why it resonates:** Security leaders want to avoid being blindsided later (“if something goes wrong in 6 months”), but engineering doesn’t want security gating adoption.

Pillar B: Dynamic attacks (AI security testing with context)

They claim they can generate **business-logic-specific attack payloads** using context inferred from the environment.



Example they gave:



* Detect system prompt uses **user input**.

* Check for input validation / guardrails.

* Attempt payload injection and measure impact based on access scope (data sensitivity, tool access).

* Produce evidence trail: chat transcript, data flow, code location, and suggested fix.

This is framed as materially better than “prompt injection scanners” that don’t understand app context.

Pillar C: Agent platform governance layer

This is the “platform” angle: integrate with agent platforms to provide a centralized view and controls:

* For each agent: tool permissions, data access, executed actions, behavioral baselines.

* Detect over-privilege (example: agent has write access to Salesforce but should be read-only).

* Provide compliance/posture reporting for leadership and board-level reporting.

They cited specific conversations with large orgs and agent-platform initiatives, including Roblox and JPMorgan Chase (and also referenced Bank of America, American Express, LinkedIn, Intuit).

* * *

4) Differentiation claim (their words, normalized)

1.  **No “heavy proxy/VPN” deployment**: they suggest alternatives rely on heavyweight inline controls (proxy/VPN) that hurt adoption.

2.  **Fast onboarding**: connect to code + cloud + agent platforms, get “first 90%” quickly.

3.  **Context-driven security efficacy**: they quoted **~85–90% efficacy** for their dynamic attacks (note: this needs validation; “efficacy” definition is unclear: precision/recall? exploit success? true-positive rate?).

* * *

5) ICP, buyer, and user (important nuance)

* **Economic buyer:** usually **CISO/CSO** or **CIO** (depends on org and whether it’s framed as security vs platform governance).

* **Primary users/workflows:** **AppSec + developers** (ticketing, fixes, Slack/engineering workflows).

* **Secondary consumers:** security leadership (reports, posture scores, board reporting templates).

This matters because Guard0 is trying to be both:

* A security leader visibility + governance system, and

* A developer/AppSec workflow engine that drives remediation.

* * *

6) Adoption psychology (what’s driving urgency)

Their strongest “why now” narrative is not “agents are scary,” it’s:

* Enterprises already have **hundreds of AI apps** (they cited one bank with ~340 AI apps by H1 2025; 80% prod).

* Board + competitive pressure is accelerating AI deployment.

* Engineering wants speed; security fears blind spots.

* Therefore, the wedge is **visibility without friction**, then expand into testing + governance.

* * *

7) GTM motion (as implied)

* Starts with POV/POC to prove discovery coverage + value quickly.

* Sells into large enterprises where platform expectation exists: land with one module, expand into platform.

They explicitly said SMBs may buy point products, but large enterprises will eventually push for a broader platform.

* * *

8) Traction and fundraising (as stated; transcription quality caveat)

Commercial signals mentioned:

* Pipeline: **~$8.5M**

* Active POVs/POCs: **~$3.5M**

* Closed: “4 deals this month” contributing “~$360k” (unclear if ARR, bookings, or TCV; needs confirmation).

* On-prem deployments: they emphasized **low marginal infra cost** and willingness to run long trials because they are “on prem” and don’t incur hosting cost.

Fundraising:

* Prior angel: **~$2M**

* Opening a **$750k** “side/extension” from interested CISOs (their framing: demand-driven).

* Seed planning: “in a month or so” (early prep).

Corporate structure:

* Brand is Guard0; Luxhan AI is the incorporated name/holding structure (per founder).


* * *

9) Competitive landscape (only what was explicitly said)

* They said they see Protect AI occasionally.

* They alluded to other players “once in a while” but the transcript is too noisy to name reliably (some competitor names were unclear).

* Their take: many buyers will not carve out “agent security” as a separate budget line unless the risk is acute; in other orgs it becomes a broader security/governance platform purchase.

* * *

10) Key diligence questions to run next (based on what they claimed)

**Product**

* What exactly powers “code + cloud sync”? (agents? scanners? log pipelines? CI integration points?)

* Coverage reality: how do they measure the “95% AI landscape” claim? What’s the denominator?

* Efficacy metrics: define 85–90% (precision/recall, exploitability hit-rate, false positives per app, etc.).

**Security posture + governance**

* Is enforcement possible (runtime gating / policy enforcement), or is it primarily discovery + reporting + ticketing?

* How do they model and manage permissions across tools and data systems (especially agent toolchains and MCP-style access)?

**GTM**

* POV structure, time-to-value, proof points that consistently convert to paid.

* Who signs: CISO vs CIO vs AppSec leader? Typical sales cycle and ACV.

* Expansion path: does the inventory wedge reliably pull through into paid testing + governance?

**Commercial**

* Clarify the “4 deals / $360k” number: ARR vs bookings vs TCV, term length, deployment mix (on-prem vs hosted).

* Customer references: which banks/enterprises are paid vs in POV (and what use case they bought first).

**Fundraise**

* Use of proceeds (engineering vs GTM vs integrations).

* What milestones they need for the seed, and what valuation/terms they’re expecting.

* * *

11) Action items from DVC side (from the end of call)

* Guard0 to send:
  
  * short deck / one-pager
  
  * demo + documentation
  
  * customer-facing materials that explain the 3 pillars clearly
* DVC to help:
  
  * design partner / buyer intros (you mentioned BFSI platform engineering teams; also Novartis as a potential network adjacency)
  
  * potentially investor intros for the $750k extension if relevant

Product does not demonstrate clear defensibility or a step-change over existing ICCC / SI-led infra software stacks. Positioning as an “AI Operating System” is broad, with functionality appearing closer to customized integrations, dashboards, and workflow automation layered on top of legacy systems rather than a differentiated core platform.

Primary risk is **buyer quality and GTM structure**. Target customers are government, defence, and public infrastructure bodies with slow procurement, heavy customization requirements, long receivable cycles, and weak software economics. Even strong delivery outcomes translate into project revenue, not repeatable, high-margin SaaS ARR.

Category is crowded with large SIs, OEM platforms, and incumbent infra software vendors, where platform ownership and pricing power sit upstream. Unclear path to product-led scale or sustained multiple expansion.

**Net:** execution-driven SI model in a difficult buyer segment, with limited product leverage. Pass.

**1. Founder & Team Background**

* Founder is **IIT Delhi alum (2013)** with **12+ years GTM + SaaS experience**

* Early entrepreneurial attempt (Gray Meter) failed due to lack of PMF → strong learning on GTM importance

* Early product leader at **LambdaTest (first 5 employees, first PM)** → deep zero-to-one SaaS exposure

* Short stint at Paytm → intentionally moved into **GTM leadership at Whatfix**

* At Whatfix, led a product from **0 → $1M ARR**, gaining hands-on pipeline + closing experience

**Co-founder (Rohan):**

* IIT Delhi CS grad

* Ex-LinkedIn (India + US), Ex-Google (US + India)

* Strong large-scale product + infra background

* Joined startup seeking faster learning & ownership

**Team Status:**

* ~15 people

* 40–50% engineering

* Lean GTM: 1 AE (founder), 1 BDR, 1 outbound specialist

**2. Problem Being Solved**

Core GTM pain points in B2B:

* **Poor pipeline quality**

* **Slow time to outreach**

* Heavy manual effort in:
  
  * Finding accounts & prospects
  
  * Cleaning & stitching data
  
  * Deep research & signal discovery
  
  * Personalization

Key challenges:

* Fragmented data vendors → low coverage + high cost

* Labor-intensive research

* LLM hallucinations → low trust

* Low adoption by BDRs (too many tools, low research skill)

Especially acute in **traditional industries** (schools, logistics, fintech, etc.) where data is sparse.

**3. Product Positioning — What Pintel Is**

**Pintel = AI-first GTM data orchestration platform**  
(Not just a lead tool, not just automation — an orchestration layer across the GTM stack)

Core capabilities:

**A. Data Orchestration**

* Acts as a **data marketplace** across multiple vendors (APAC, EMEA, US)

* Proprietary ingestion of **unstructured data (websites, directories, job pages)**

* Solves vendor fragmentation + coverage issues

**B. Workflow-Driven AI Agents**

* Custom GTM workflows via **no-code prompts**

* Specialized agents per use case:
  
  * Account prioritization
  
  * Prospect research
  
  * Contact discovery
  
  * Signal detection

Key innovation:

* Converts **raw account lists → context-rich, scored target accounts**

* Users define **custom signals + weightages** (cloud spend, FinOps presence, hiring, etc.)

**C. Deep Integration (Adoption Moat)**

* Runs **inside CRM & sales tools** (Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach, dialers)

* SDRs never log into Pintel → zero adoption friction

* API connector allows integration with any sales tool

**D. End-to-End Coverage**

* Outbound:
  
  * Account selection
  
  * Prospect discovery
  
  * Talking tracks for cold calls
  
  * Messaging personalization
* Inbound:
  
  * Auto-qualifies signups
  
  * Enriches using just email domain
  
  * Prioritizes high-intent leads

Net effect:

* Faster outreach

* Higher relevance

* Less human dependency

* Higher pipeline quality

**4. Competitive Positioning**

Pintel does **not replace** Apollo / ZoomInfo initially — it **coexists and orchestrates on top**.

Current stack before Pintel:

* ZoomInfo / Apollo → raw lists

* LinkedIn Sales Nav → prospecting

* Manual research → filtering

* CRM → execution

With Pintel:

* Automates the **middle intelligence layer**:
  
  * Context generation
  
  * Signal detection
  
  * Scoring
  
  * Personalization

Founder positioning:

* Long-term replacing **large parts of the sales tech stack**

* Becomes the **“business logic layer” for GTM AI agents**

**5. Traction & Customers**

**Product launched:** July 2025 (≈ 2 quarters old)

**Current metrics:**

* **Customers:** 15+ paying

* Strong expansion from initial design partners

**Notable customers:**

* CoreStack

* Maxio (US)

* Knox

**GTM performance:**

* 5–7 new meetings per week (US-heavy)

* 20–30 new meetings per month

Outbound has been primary motion — using Pintel internally.

**Current motion:** Sales-led outbound  
**Next phase:** Add **PLG** from Feb onward

Founder’s view:

* Sales-led = consistent growth

* PLG = nonlinear flywheel

* Goal: **$1M → $10M ARR very fast**

Verticals:

Here are the key points from the conversation:

1.  **Feature Request for Dynamic Sampling**: There’s a need for the ability to change sampling percentages on the fly without restarting agents, a feature not easily available in current tools.

2.  **Observability for AI Agents**: Traditional observability tools (e.g., Fiddler) are not yet equipped for the complexity of AI-driven agents, which require tracking interactions and decision-making processes, not just model performance.

3.  **Custom Data Lake for Observability**: The company had to build its own data lake and distributed query engine due to limitations with tools like ClickHouse. They designed a system that efficiently handles hybrid search (full-text, analytical, and time-series) at high data volumes.

4.  **Cost-Effective Solution**: The product offers significant cost savings (70-90%) compared to existing solutions like ElasticSearch and CloudWatch, with faster query performance, targeting Series A customers.

5.  **Fundraising & Expansion Plans**: The company is raising $1.2 million to scale operations, especially in the U.S. market. They are focused on hiring engineers for further development, especially in vector search and AI-specific observability.

6.  **Market & VC Challenges**: The company faces difficulties in raising funds due to being registered in India, limiting access to U.S.-based investors. There\'s a need for cross-border investor support to access U.S. market opportunities.

7.  **Investor Feedback**: VCs suggest increasing ACVs, targeting larger customers, and expanding cross-border connections. They recommend focusing on customer feedback and connecting with the right networks to scale effectively.

8.  **Next Steps**: Plans to review the company’s deck and whitepaper, followed by a follow-up call to discuss potential collaboration and further investor connections.

Recent informal discussions held with developers and engineering leads across **Amazon, Pega Systems, Nutanix, Rippling, and Salesforce** to gauge the adoption dynamics and pain points around QA automation and test-case generation tools.



**Key Insights from Developer Conversations**

* **Developers own testing:**  
  Across all large-scale enterprises, developers themselves **write and maintain test cases** as part of their CI/CD workflows. Dedicated QA teams focus more on integration, compliance, and regression validation rather than generating new cases.

* **Existing tools suffice:**  
  Most teams rely on **internal frameworks + general-purpose AI coding assistants** (Claude, Copilot, etc.) to create or refine test cases. These fit naturally within developer workflows and IDEs.

* **Low demand for new QA tools:**  
  Introduction of new QA platforms typically requires **strong top-down buy-in** and long procurement cycles. QA/DevOps stack changes are infrequent and rarely initiated bottom-up.

* **Enterprise inertia:**  
  Once testing infrastructure is embedded (Jenkins, JUnit, Selenium, etc.), switching costs and integration risk make replacement unattractive unless there’s a **10× productivity gain**.

**Market Implications**

* **Enterprise GTM is difficult:**  
  Selling into large enterprises will require **heavy top-down motion** (CIO/CTO-driven) and long sales cycles. Individual developers are unlikely to champion a new QA platform.

* **Likely SMB play:**  
  The **core opportunity lies in SMB and mid-market** engineering teams that lack mature internal QA pipelines and are more open to adopting plug-and-play tools.

**Numocity – Call Notes (Karthik Conversation)**



* * *

**1️ Market Structure & Charging Model Evolution**

**CaaS Scaling From 1% → 10%**

Karthik highlighted that **Charging-as-a-Service (CaaS)** has meaningfully scaled in the last ~24–30 months, driven primarily by fleet electrification.  
CaaS is now ~10% of the market, up from ~1% three years ago.

Key drivers include:

* Rapid electrification of delivery and ride-hailing fleets (e-2W, e-3W cargo, early e-4W fleets).

* Shift from hardware sales to **selling uptime & managed charging sessions**.

* Emergence of capex-light fleet-focused models (depot charging, pay-per-use, managed charging).

**Implication:**  
CaaS only works when operators can push utilization to **25–40%+** or control the fleet themselves.  
This explains why it is maturing in fleet-heavy pockets but still early for retail.

* * *

**2️ Utilization Reality & System Constraints**

**15–20% Today → 30% Long-Term Ceiling**

Karthik sees a mature utilization ceiling of ~30% for India, which aligns with global patterns in early-stage EV markets.

Structural constraints include:

* Long dwell times even on DCFC (30–50 minutes).

* Charging demand highly concentrated during morning/evening peaks.

* Strong home/office charging preference limiting public demand.

India currently has ~13–15k public chargers vs ~40–50k required for density parity.

**Implication:**  
Large networks will be locked to a structural utilization ceiling unless highway traffic, apartment restrictions, and fleet EV penetration rise meaningfully.

* * *

**3️ Home Charging Dominance & Its Impact on Public Infra**

Home charging delivers **3–4× cheaper** unit economics vs public fast charging.  
As a result, public charging behaves like a **top-up or convenience** market, not a primary charging mode.

Public chargers today mostly serve:

* Fleet vehicles

* Highway top-ups

* Apartment residents without dedicated parking

* Emergency use-cases

Retail adoption is slow because >95% of charging occurs at home/office.

* * *

**4️ Fleet-Centric Load Is the Real Driver for Public Charging**

Fleets (ride-hailing, delivery, logistics) charge **2–3× per day**, creating natural demand for public and semi-public infra.

Examples cited showed 70–85% utilization only when **the operator controls both EVs + charging infra**.

Retail environments cannot replicate this.

* * *

**5️ Urban Trip Profiles Explain Low Public Charger Usage**

Observations:

* Typical daily urban travel: **15–22 km/day**.

* Overnight slow charging meets most personal needs.

* EV penetration remains low outside top 8 metros.

Thus, public chargers remain underutilized except in highways and commercial hubs.

* * *

**6️ Office Parking (OFC) Emerging as a Stable Semi-Public Segment**

Corporate campuses and tech parks are becoming the “new home charging” for many EV users.

Reasons:

* 6–8 hour dwell times match AC slow charger economics.

* Corporates pushing employee EV policies.

* Plannable daytime load → higher utilization vs malls/retail.

* * *

**7️ Apartment Safety Norms as a Demand Tailwind**

RWAs are increasingly restricting unsafe socket charging due to fire risk.

This pushes residents toward:

* Managed & metered shared charging

* Basement/ground floor semi-public AC charging

* Dedicated EV panels installed by DISCOMs

Medium-term, this is a structural tailwind for managed charging software platforms.

* * *

**8️ Charging Speed Upgradation Will Be Slow**

Most infra is still **7–22 kW AC**, and widespread DC fast-charging (60–180 kW) requires:

* Grid upgrades

* Cooling systems

* Higher capex and coordination with DISCOMs

So improvement from “8 hours → 1 hour” will be gradual.

* * *

**9️ Public Charging ROI Hierarchy**

Ranking mentioned:

**Highways >> Office Parking >> Malls**

* Highways: predictable long-distance use cases; high willingness to pay.

* OFC: reliable dwell times; good economics for AC charging.

* Malls: weekend-heavy, unpredictable, lower throughput.

Note: Highway infra rollout is **still slow**, delaying ROI in the most attractive segment.

* * *

**1️0 SEA Market Comparison**

Karthik sees SEA markets (Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam) tracking similar utilization curves (~10–20%).

**Exception:** Singapore → higher density + strict home charging constraints → higher public usage.

**Interpretation:**  
SEA is primarily a **2W-heavy** region, making India’s 4W-centric orchestration market less comparable.

* * *

**1️1 Roaming: Low Take Rates (2–3%) + OEM Incentives**

Roaming penetration remains extremely low (~2–3%) because:

* India’s charging networks lack deep OCPI-based interoperability.

* OEMs prefer **captive charging ecosystems** to control user data, safety, and upsell channels.

This slows the emergence of a unified charging network.

* * *

**1️2 Timeline to Reach 15–20% Public Charging Penetration**

Karthik estimates **5–7 years** for public charging to reach ~15–20% of total charging sessions (from today’s ~4–6%).

Prerequisites:

* Apartment-level electrification

* Dense highway networks

* Cost reduction in DC fast charging

* Larger share of buyers without home parking

* Broad-based 4W EV adoption

* * *

**1️3 Numocity-Specific Strategic Considerations Raised by Karthik**

**Dependency on 4W Uptick**

Numocity’s product is strongest in **e-4W, fleet, depot, and enterprise CPO** environments.  
However, 4W EV adoption in India is capex-heavy and subsidy-dependent → delays Numocity’s fastest-growing segment.

**Highway Growth Will Be Slow Despite Being Attractive**

Highways are the highest ROI segment but the **slowest to build out**, delaying scale for highway-centric customers.

**SEA Not Ideal; Middle East May Be Stronger**

SEA = 2W dominant → less aligned with Numocity’s enterprise-grade orchestration layer.  
Middle East = utility-driven infra + faster centralized rollouts → potentially better fit.

**Tata Group Discussions Not Materialized Yet**

Numocity has been in discussions with **Tata Power** and possibly **Tata EV**, but nothing has advanced to a commercial stage.  
This is critical since Tata accounts for **70%+ of 4W EVs** in India.

**OEM Partnerships Today Are Low-Market-Share**

Existing OEM integrations (Audi, Skoda, GM, Kia) have limited impact due to minimal EV share in India.  
Partnership value will meaningfully shift only when larger OEMs (Tata, MG, Hyundai, Mahindra) onboard.

**Numocity – Call Notes (Kunjan Conversation)**

* * *

**1️ Product Architecture & Strategic Analogies**

* **Telecom Parallel:**  
  Kunjan drew a strong analogy to telecom OSS/BSS systems — specifically how telecom networks manage **pulse reading**, endpoint signaling, uptime routing, and protocol interoperability.  
  Numocity plays a similar orchestration role for EV chargers, ensuring consistent communication between hardware, users, and the grid.

* **Prism Payments (ATM Switching) Analogy:**  
  He mapped Numocity to **Prism Payments**, which sat as the invisible switching layer powering ATMs.  
  Numocity serves as the “middleware” operating layer that enables charging sessions, billing, uptime, roaming, and asset orchestration — sitting beneath the consumer interface but critical for infra reliability.

* **Hardware/Chemistry Agnostic:**  
  Completely independent of battery chemistry, BMS type, and charger OEM — enabling universal operability across markets.

* **Dynamic Charging Control:**  
  Software can dynamically alter charging speed, balance loads, and react to battery/grid conditions, positioning the product closer to EV infra orchestration rather than basic CMS functionality.

* * *

**2️ Customer Base, Monetization & Market Dynamics**

* **Oligopolistic Buyers:**  
  Market primarily consists of utilities, large CPOs, and energy infrastructure players who often operate in regional oligopolies.  
  This typically creates **low price elasticity** for the core software layer and supports enterprise-grade pricing.


* * *

**3️ Market Evolution & Growth Drivers**

* **Trucking and Depot Charging:**  
  Kunjan sees heavy-duty trucking as a major upcoming market.  
  Depot charging requires high uptime, intelligent load management, and predictive routing — areas where Numocity has advantage due to its orchestration layer.

* **US Entry via Smart Meter Networks:**  
  Landis+Gyr–style smart meter ecosystems could serve as a natural route into the US market, since metering infrastructures are closely tied to EV charger integration.

* * *

**4️ Pricing, Value, and Stickiness**

* **Pricing Range:**  
  Enterprise deals between **$50K to $500K**, depending on licensing scope and device/user volume.

* **Value Drivers:**
  
  * Charger uptime
  
  * Accurate revenue metering
  
  * Load balancing
  
  * Operational transparency for CPOs
  
  * Billing + settlement reliability
* **Stickiness:**  
  Once integrated with chargers, payments, and field-support workflows, switching becomes highly costly — creating long-term entrenchment.

* * *

**5️ EV Adoption Outlook**

* **Steady, Not Explosive:**  
  Kunjan expects EV penetration to climb steadily rather than in sudden spikes.

* **Improving Range & Model Diversity:**  
  With 350–400 km ranges becoming common and more brands visible on roads (Tata, BYD, Tesla, MG, Hyundai), consumer adoption will gradually accelerate.

* **Long-Term Category:**  
  This category should be viewed on a **10+ year horizon**, not a 3–5 year startup hypergrowth cycle.  
  Market will structurally shift from ICE to EV over a decade, giving infra software players long but patient ramps.

**Key Insights from Raja – Manch Evaluation (Aug 21)**

1\. **Positioning & Market Fit**

* The platform makes sense primarily for **enterprises with large onboarding structures** and multiple vendors.

* It is not a **full-fledged MDM solution**; instead, it acts as an **extension to onboarding before MDM systems like Informatica, Ataccama, etc.**

* In enterprises, **MDM and onboarding are distinct systems**; in smaller firms, they may be bundled.

* Competitors exist in the **KYC onboarding and workflow automation** space; Manch must differentiate clearly.

2\. **Strengths**

* Built solid **KYC + workflow + rule engine capabilities**.

* Good **customer logos** (Pepsi, Coca-Cola, Swiggy, Pidilite, UPL Fertilizers, etc.) and adoption in multiple countries.

* Advantage of **early adoption** and ground reality knowledge from customer experience.

* Team has worked hard and evolved capabilities over time.

3\. **Weaknesses / Concerns**

* **Not unique** in KYC — multiple platforms exist. Positioning solely as a “KYC company” risks commoditization.

* Heavy reliance on **marketing/GTM partnerships** — organic growth seems limited.

* **Scalability to true enterprise-level MDM** is questionable. Currently more mid-market than enterprise-grade.

* **Partnership claims** (with large firms) not validated yet — risk of overstating traction.

* Technology seen as **buildable by others** (OCR, document parsing, onboarding workflows are replicable).

4\. **Team Assessment**

* **Suresh** (founder) is good with customers and product experience but **~60% technically sound** compared to peers in data/MDM (e.g., DQLabs).

* Strong on execution and customer management, but **not CTO-level technical depth**.

* No significant **AI differentiation** beyond standard document parsing/OCR.

5\. **Investment View (Raja’s perspective)**

* Would not invest personally:
  
  * Reliant on strong marketing to scale, not organic pull.
  
  * Risk of being displaced quickly by bigger players.
  
  * Needs more GTM partners to drive growth.
* **DVC could add value** by leveraging its network, but without strong organic growth, sustainability is a concern.

* Suggested short-term rather than long-term investment horizon if pursued.

**Next Steps Suggested**

* Validate **partnership claims**.

* Benchmark against **other KYC + onboarding platforms** globally.

* Request **demos or technical deep dives** to assess true product differentiation.



In short, Raja sees Manch as a capable KYC/onboarding workflow platform with strong logos but **not a true MDM player**, with **scalability, positioning, and technical depth concerns**. Heavy reliance on marketing/GTM raises sustainability risks.

Technical due diligence review for Mojo platform scalability and architecture

Thu, 29 Jan 26

Technical Due Diligence Overview

* DD process involved 4-5 calls (1-1.5 hours each) with Mojo’s CTO and CEO
  
  * Covered product demos, technical architecture discussions
  
  * Team was forthcoming about perceived product issues
  
  * Detailed technical notes maintained with AI assistant summaries
* Assessment follows structured format used for other DD processes

* No code review or artifact inspection conducted - interview-based approach

Architecture Assessment

* **Overall verdict**: Reasonably sensible architecture with no major red flags

* Reactive event-driven microservices architecture
  
  * Modular design enables both infrastructure and team scaling
  
  * Problem decomposed into manageable components
* Optimization algorithm structured in 3 parts:
  
  1.  Problem decomposition - orders clustered by optimization needs/zones
  
  2.  Parallel optimization - uses meta-heuristic approach (not mixed integer programming)
  
  3.  Solution assembly - reconciles all parts into single plan
* Current deployment: Region-wise (US and Southeast Asia) with stateless services

* Data stack: Postgres (operational), Elasticsearch (analytics/time series), Kafka (events)

* Team size: ~20 engineers total

Key Gaps & Scalability Concerns

* **QA automation missing** - currently manual due to use case complexity
  
  * Team aware and planning to add QA automation team soon
  
  * **Limited observability** - especially for core optimization engine
  
  * Infrastructure monitoring exists (using Zoho 24/7, migrating to Grafana)
  
  * Application-level observability weak - difficult to trace algorithm behavior
  
  * Could impact troubleshooting speed at scale
* **Multi-tenancy risks** - shared operational DB and Elasticsearch
  
  * Large customer spikes could impact others in same region
  
  * Requires proper resource planning
* **Self-managed infrastructure** - may need heavy infra team lifting at scale
  
  * Could migrate to managed cloud services (Azure)
  
  
Next Steps

* Team to review detailed technical report

* Reconvene early next week with specific questions

* Potential follow-up: synthetic data testing of optimization algorithms if needed

NEXT STEPS

2.  Gokul Dixit: Compose 4-5 specific questions for CMOs globally to gather insights on marketer perspectives, consumer trends, and player performance in the shoppable video and social commerce space.

The platform allows brands to search for relevant content, manage user rights, and deploy shoppable media across various touchpoints.

1.  Shoppable video and social commerce


\- The discussion centered on the potential of shoppable video to transform consumer experiences and close the purchase funnel more effectively. Shalini noted that while everyone agrees on its potential, adoption outside of China has been slower than anticipated. The group explored use cases in retail environments, social media, and connected TV platforms.

\- There were questions raised about the readiness of consumers to make quick purchasing decisions through these new formats, especially in markets outside China. The conversation touched on the need to understand how these tools fit into the broader consumer purchase journey across different market segments.

1.  Competitor landscape

Shalini mentioned her experience with companies like Madstreet Dann, which despite raising significant funding, had not scaled as expected in the fashion tech space. The group noted that while there are multiple players, Live2AI claims to offer a more comprehensive solution that has allowed them to replace competitors at some client accounts.

1.  Market adoption and consumer behavior


\- There was significant discussion around the pace of adoption for shoppable video and social commerce tools. Shalini shared her experience at Nykaa, where despite significant investment in live commerce, consumer readiness and ROI were challenges. The group explored differences in adoption across markets, with China being seen as more advanced in this space.

\- Questions were raised about the sustainability of these tools as revenue channels for brands, particularly in the face of economic downturns when discretionary spending might be cut. The team discussed the need for more data on consumer engagement and conversion rates to better understand the true impact of these technologies.

1.  Technical differentiation and integration


\- The conversation touched on Live2AI\'s technical capabilities and how they differentiate from competitors. Shyam highlighted that Live2AI offers a pure software solution, unlike some competitors that rely heavily on services. The platform\'s ability to manage thousands of social media handles from a single interface was noted as a key differentiator.

1.  Business model and financials

There was mention of a $100,000 minimum per account and discussion of the company\'s success in expanding contracts, such as growing from $20,000 to $360,000 with Henkel. The potential total addressable market (TAM) within single large clients like Henkel was estimated to be significant, though realistically capturing the full TAM was seen as challenging.

1.  Potential challenges and concerns


\- Several concerns were raised during the discussion. These included questions about the defensibility of Live2AI\'s technology, the pace of market adoption, integration challenges for enterprise clients, and the potential for in-house development of similar capabilities by large tech-savvy companies. Shalini cautioned about the long sales cycles and the need for extensive piloting and validation before large-scale adoption by enterprise clients.

\- The team also discussed the importance of understanding the true impact on consumer behavior and purchase decisions, as well as the need for more data on engagement and conversion rates to justify investment in these technologies.

Meeting Notes - Board Meeting - 28th OCtober-2025

MINUTES 1. The meeting kicked off with Suman providing the financial updates for the month of September. Revenue and expense numbers for the month were brought up and discussed. The burn & expenses were below the AOP thresholds. 2. The board congratulated iTuring for crossing the 1 crore Monthly Revenue mark for the first time. The Half yearly Revenue was also close to the AOP targets. 3. The progress on the Sales & Marketing engine was discussed. It was highlighted that the Sales & Marketing engine is now ready, and inbound leads have started coming in. Suman highlighted the various top of the funnel opportunities across India, US & SA. Major banking sector pilots in South Africa & life insurance opportunities in India were discussed. 4. Board members pointed out the need for patience in B2B enterprise sales, especially in Banking sector in India & elsewhere. It was highlighted that only a larger top of the funnel can help counter the unpredictability of enterprise deals. 5. The various efforts being undertaken to expand the top of the funnel were highlighted by Suman & Valsan. The American Banking Association (ABA) Conference and the various interests received in Banking & Credit Unions’ space were highlighted. It was also informed that iTuring will be attending the Chicago Collections Conference & is now a member of American Collection Association. 6. It was mentioned that the hiring had been slow in the near past as a deliberate move to allow full mobilization of the Sales & Marketing engine. Now that the engine has started to generate leads and the collections product is nearing launch, the hiring will be ramped up. 7. It was agreed upon by all members that the sales & marketing conversations need to be centered around the funnel. With the engine in place, it was informed that HubSpot is now being used by the sales team, & the executive dashboards are being cleaned to exclude old records & present credible, updated numbers. It is expected that the Executive dashboards will be presented to the board by the next week. 8. Board members highlighted the need for presenting not just the actuals vs AOP metrics but also the quarter-to-quarter & month-to-month shifts in financials, funnel & customer accounts to enable a more focused discussion on iTuring’s growth journey. With the use case driven vertical products now coming into the picture, future MIS meetings would also benefit from the addition of product line to reporting & forecasting paradigms. 9. Partha informed the members that he would be sharing a presentation template to structure future financial & Sales Funnel discussions. This would help reduce the time spent on operational discussions and enable more focus on strategic support that can be provided by the board members. 10. A particular point of discussion was iTuring’s use-case based “Land & Expand” strategy, combining its predictive platform capabilities with Agentic AI to serve three main use cases: (a) Customer Acquisition (including deposit growth, which was a particular demand expressed by banking stakeholders during the ABA conference), (b) Credit Underwriting & (c) Collections. 11. Collections use-case was identified as the current focus area, with the Agentic based Collections Product nearing completion. It was highlighted that the Collections product launch is being planned in the near short term, and a promotional product video (which had garnered particular attention from ABA attendees) was also shown to the board. 12. Board members were highly aligned with the use case driven product vision, and the market research & strategic vision behind Collections product was discussed. Various market insights, product market fit, and AI based value propositions were shared.

AGENDA



1.  Understand Cyborg\'s product and partnership with Fiserv

2.  Evaluate revenue model and applicability of solutions

3.  Provide feedback on market viability



KEY HIGHLIGHTS



1.  Cyborg has signed a partnership with Fiserv to provide accounts payable automation for Fiserv\'s merchants using Cyborg\'s risk models




1.  The partnership originated through Sri Wilson, ex-Fiserv executive, who helped secure the deal and has now joined Cyborg as a co-founder to head US sales




1.  Cyborg competes with SAS, H2O.ai and DataRobot by providing tailored ML models and faster deployment targeted for BFSI companies




1.  80% of Cyborg\'s revenue comes from platform-as-a-service with 5 year contracts, 20% from API-as-a-service based on usage




NEXT STEPS



1.  Akhil Lukose: Share details on existing customer use cases leveraging Cyborg\'s models and platform

2.  Akhil Lukose: Provide customer references and facilitate reference calls to validate product-market fit

3.  Suresh Kumar: Review Cyborg\'s capabilities applicable for Onbe\'s needs after more details available



TOPICS DISCUSSED



1.  Cyborg\'s partnership with Fiserv




\- Cyborg has signed a partnership with Fiserv\'s Snappay business unit to provide accounts payable automation using risk models, targeting 180 Fiserv customers with $4B annual transactions

\- The partnership aims to reduce default rates from 2% to 1%, driving cost savings

\- Sri Wilson secured the Fiserv partnership before joining Cyborg as a co-founder to lead US sales given his strong connections



1.  Cyborg\'s product capabilities and offerings




\- Cyborg provides a platform for data teams to gather, clean, analyze data and deploy models targeted for BFSI companies

\- Key functionality is around risk modeling and assessment across insurance, lending, accounts payable etc.

\- They have over 25,000 prebuilt models and capabilties for faster model deployment and tuning

\- The platform is not a workflow automation solution but focused on risk analysis



1.  Cyborg\'s target customers and market positioning




\- Cyborg is targeting BFSI companies with specialized data products vs. horizontal AI platforms from competitors

\- Existing customers are primarily Indian banks, with early international expansion planned through the Fiserv partnership

\- Long term plan is to be a leader in BFSI-focused AI capabilities combined with strong ML tooling



1.  Revenue model and pricing strategy of Cyborg




\- 80% of revenue comes from fixed fee 5 year platform-as-a-service contracts

\- 20% revenue from usage based API-as-a-service, expected to see strong growth

\- API services would require integration with customer systems to feed data and consume risk analysis



1.  Applicability of Cyborg\'s solutions for Onbe




\- Depends on the specific risk modeling use cases where Cyborg has productized capabilities vs. one-off consulting solutions

\- Onbe is exploring similar fraud analysis solutions e.g. with Effectv

\- Needs clear understanding of the domain expertise and prebuilt models Cyborg can leverage for Onbe

\- They are expected to maintain differentiation lead though space may get more competitive.

\- The current round aims to sustain for 18 months during which Zybor expects to grow from sub $1M to $2-3M revenue.



1.  Fund raising plans




\- The current $4-5M round is a Series round, not bridge. It will provide 18 months runway for growth.

\- Another round expected in 6 months to power further growth while maintaining reasonable valuations and dilution for existing investors.



1.  Exit opportunities




\- Strong possibility of exit for investors in 2-3 years time frame via M&A by companies like SAS, Fiserv itself, financial institutions or product companies wanting AI differentiation.

\- This phase is crucial for value multiplication so M&A in next 6 months may not give best outcome for investors.



1.  Key performance indicators




\- Main KPIs tracked are related to financial performance. Granular tracking of product KPIs not done much.

\- The bootstrapped founder is financially prudent regarding cash burn so growth opportunities have to be assessed accordingly.



1.  Interest received in current fundraise




\- Good interest from multiple sizable funds for the current round.



1.  Need for deep tech investor




\- No strong need felt for deep tech investor as Sumit seems adept at understanding industry needs and product requirements.

**In-person meeting between Shyam and Anshul & Saurav in Redwood City, CA on 11th Oct 2025:**  
  
I met Anshul Shrivastava and Kumar Saurav – both of them are co-founders of Vodex on 11th Oct in Redwood City - CA.   
  
Here is my notes:  
  
**Product/Market:**  
  
1. They are focusing on Collections domain with a primary focus on US. If I remember right, they mentioned they have around 7 customers in the US.   
2. Most of these customers are acquired through direct/focused reach out either through LIn or events  
3. Both the founders are sending good amount of time in the US – travelling and staying in US for few weeks every quarter

4.Currently they have B1 visa, but they are trying to get L1 visa and move to US on permanent basis.



**Founders:**

1.  I believe both of them are first time founders.

2.  US market is very new to them. I think they are very raw for a US GTM. At the same time, I also think they have a pretty good start in the US – having 7 US customers is pretty good start.

3.  They need to learn a lot about US GTM and also understand the US culture and professionalism to succeed in the US market.

4.  Anshul is focusing on Sales and GTM and Saurav is focusing on Product and Technology



**Structure:**

1.  They said they are seriously exploring moving their entity to US.

2.  If they are US domiciled with US focused GTM, we may have to pass this deal to our US team.



**Synergies:**  
1. I asked them about Cyborg/iTuring (IT) – they said IT is still doing POC/integrations and hasn’t yet become a paying customer. So, I don’t think we should give too much weightage to Cyborg relation at this time. We need to wait and see on how this spans out.   
2. They said they don’t know who Valsan is. I met Valsan one day before I met Vodex founders. Valsan also mentioned to me that IT is now focusing on Collections vertical in the US as they got initial success in that area.   
3. I think there could be pretty good synergies between IT and Vodex from US GTM perspective. We should check with Suman and make intros to Vodex founders and Valsan and ask them to explore any joint GTM etc. Vodex has more customers in US than IT at this time.   
  
**Next Steps:**

1.Have a call with them to understand their revenue numbers and sales pipeline.

1.  Check with them on their domicile strategy and pass the deal to US team if they want to move to US.

2.  They may say they want to raise current round in India and move to US to later round. We need to think if DVC India should invest in such a case as this would have complications from SEBI macro quota when they change the domicile and I am not sure what are the complications and cost for us to do it.  
    4. Connect them with Valan to explore GTM synergies in Collections domain in the US.

1.  iTuring is integrating Vodex Voice AI into their solution and thinks it is a good fit for DVC investment

2.  He will futher evaluate their tech moat and give a feedback in 2 weeks @Ashok Rampalli pls add in pipeline

3.  Vodex is a Pentathlon PC and they dont want to raise money now but Suman is convincing them to take DVC money

4.  They are using Deepgram foundational model and have shown good use cases

5.  ARR $750K and looking to reach $1M.

GoBoon is a referral-hiring platform that turns employee and external networks into automated talent pipelines, promising faster, cheaper hires than job boards and generic ATS referral modules.

* * *

2\. Team

* **Dakota Younger (CEO, Co-Founder):** Ex-recruiter; deep TA domain knowledge;

* **Gary Epper (Co-Founder):** HR / ops background.  
  **Diligence gap:** Need detail on engineering leadership, prior exits, and GTM bench.

* * *

3\. Traction (Site-Reported)  
**Note:** No public ARR / NRR; needs data-room validation.

* * *

4\. Product & Tech

* Converts every job into a referral campaign across **employees + external contacts**.

* Gamified incentives (points, leaderboards) to sustain referrer engagement.

* Integration-first: plugs into existing ATS (Greenhouse, Lever, etc.) and comms (Slack/Teams/WhatsApp).  
  **Edge: Speed of deployment + external referral graph vs. typical “employee-only” referral tools.**

* * *

6\. Competitors

* **Direct referral platforms:** Teamable, RolePoint.

* **ATS with referral modules:** Greenhouse, Lever, Workable, iCIMS.  
  **Positioning:** “Best-in-class referral layer” vs. bundled, slower, less engaging ATS add-ons.

* * *

7\. Key Highlights

* Clear ROI narrative (faster, cheaper hires, better quality).

* Very fast implementation + deep integrations → low friction wedge.

* Real network-effect potential if external referral graph scales.

**Notes from call with Sourabh Nolkha - Ex VP Finance at ITILITE - 18/Oct/2023**



**Participants:**



DVC - Shyam and Gokul

Saurabh Nolkha - [https://www.linkedin.com/in/sourabh-nolkha-76a8402a/][1]



Sourabh is Shyam\'s connect through ISB. He worked as head of Finance at Itilite earlier.



DICE guys mentioned that Itilite is one of their competitor in the travel area.



Notes:

\* It will be difficult to sell a product in India if it has only Expense Management module. For Expense management, ₹20 per employee per month is a reasonable pricing

\*. Travel Module - Itilite has lot of travel agents on its payroll. How much ever you automate the ticketing process, you are bound to see failures. These agents work on resolving such issues. Since ITILITE takes care of end to end travel process for its clients, this is required. Check with DICE how they are resolving these failures.

\* You get around 5 of the ticket prices as commission if you own the inventory. If you don\'t own the inventory, you may get 1. If you have to make ₹20 Lacs a month on Travel, you need to process a GMC of ₹20 Crores a month. This is huge volume. Validate this with DICE and how they are going to make money on Travel module.

\* For AP module, average price in India is around ₹8 to **₹**10 per invoice.

\* Selling Expense Management alone is a big challenge - you need to sell it along with Travel or AP to make it attractive

\* All 3 modules - Travel, Expense Management and AP are commoditised ( Saurabh may be looking more from a processing point of view and may not be from s/w or SaaS point of vie)

\* Itilite raised $29M in Apr 2022 - Saurabh left them few months before this. As per Tracxn, they got a valuation of $155M (Post) when their revenues were just ₹11.2 Crores. When I asked his opinion on this round, Sourabh mentioned Itilite raised this round saying they will go international. He thinks that the revenues should have picked up a lot due to this. We need to wait for Tracxn to update this data may be in Nov/Dec after they file their returns.

**Business Performance & Growth**

* **ARR doubled** from ~$800K in August to **~$1.6M** now.

* **Quarterly Performance:**
  
  * **Q2 was strong**, Q4 had weak pipeline but decent closures.
  
  * **Q1 looking good** with some deals delayed; early signs of better performance.
* **Strategic Shift:** Moving upmarket — exploring longer sales cycles and more complex buying journeys.

**Strategic Partnerships**

**1. Zuora**

* **Closed a deep go-to-market + equity partnership**.

* Zuora sunsetting its underperforming *Zuora Collect* ($25M revenue) and promoting Growfin instead.

* **Partnership scope:**
  
  * Revenue-share GTM.
  
  * Growfin provides tech + services; Zuora handles GTM.
  
  * Positioned as *invoice-to-cash* complement to Zuora’s *quote-to-invoice*.
* **Equity investment** by Zuora: $5M via convertible note at **$50M post-money cap**.

* Zuora initially wanted equity via Shopify-style model (without capital), which Growfin declined.

**2. NetSuite**

* **Formal GTM partnership** established.

* **Mutual benefits:**
  
  * NetSuite wants GenAI-native partners.
  
  * Growfin becomes part of their co-marketing and referral programs.
* Running **joint events/webinars**, tapping into NetSuite’s reseller and alliance ecosystem.

* Partnership led by **Head of Partnerships** with deep ties to NetSuite.

**Team Expansion & US Plans**

* Current Sales Team: **3 AEs based in India**.

* Hiring a **Head of Sales in the US** – closure expected by May.

* Founder moving to **Bay Area (South Bay)** around **Aug-Sep 2025**; family to follow later due to school cycle.

**Fundraise Details**

* **Structure:** Convertible note.

* **Amount Raised:** $5M solely from Zuora.

* **Valuation Cap:** $50M post-money.

* **No board seat** granted to maintain neutrality.

* Deferred participation from existing investors to future priced round (likely Series B).

**Founder Learnings & Strategic Shifts**

* Partnership + fundraise process was **intense, time-consuming (~5 months)** and involved deep diligence:
  
  * Codebase, architecture, scaling capabilities.
  
  * Customer references (Zuora spoke to 10–12 handpicked ones).
  
  * Multiple internal stakeholders at Zuora evaluated the deal.
* Gained key experience negotiating with strategic corporates and balancing equity/funding alignment.

**AI Adoption & Internal Productivity Boost**

* Inspired by **SaaSBOOMi** learnings:
  
  * Pushing AI adoption across internal functions.
  
  * Using **Cursor.ai** and **Prisma.ai** to speed up development.
* Built internal dashboards and POCs with dramatically faster dev cycles.

* Focused on **AI productivity → not hiring → tools instead**.

* Cautious around LLM-based core product use due to performance/security concerns.

**Future Fundraising Considerations**

* No immediate plans to raise — board discussion pending.

* Debating between:
  
  * **Top-up** round vs.
  
  * Full **Series B** priced round later in the year.
* Conscious of shifting Series B expectations:
  
  * Stronger traction, AI story, sales efficiency, and retention now critical.

Mail sent to Aarvind \" Hi Aravind. Thanks for sharing everything.

We did have a chance to review and discuss internally.

I think at this stage it is best to hold off and revisit when you are ready for Series A. I understand we are taking a risk of not having enough allocation for us but that is a chance unfortunately we have to take. We would definitely be very interested at that point given the goals you plant to achieve by then.

The reason for holding off is mainly because I think our perspectives on how to structure this are too far apart. It doesn\'t mean you are wrong but it just doesn\'t work for us.

For the sake of maintaining a good relationship with you and 314, we should stay in touch and chat again later this year.

We do think highly of you and the opportunity ahead of Growfin and of course I am happy to help in any way possible in the meantime.

I also had a call this morning with Nruthya and Anurag and communicated the same message.

Talk soon.\"

**/Market Segmentation and Challenges**

Primary Focus: Generating invoices and accepting digital payments.

Common Solutions: Lightweight tools integrated with QuickBooks, Xero, Zoho Books, etc. Examples include Bill.com, Invoice2go, etc.

Challenges: Transition from simple invoicing to handling various customer types, payment methods, terms, and invoicing models.



**Why Mid-Market Companies?**

Managing more complex invoicing and payment processes, integrating with ERP systems like NetSuite, Sage, Microsoft Dynamics.

Sometimes use ERP for invoicing or specialized billing systems like Chargebee or Zuora for subscriptions.

Challenges: Complex workflows from quote to invoicing, handling various business models (transactional, subscription, usage-based, services, contract-based), and integrating multiple payment and invoicing systems.



**Other players vs Growfin**

Custom-built solutions on top of robust ERPs (SAP, Oracle) with help from large service providers (Infosys, TCS, Accenture).

High Radius, GetPaid, etc., which integrate deeply with ERP systems.

Challenges: Long implementation cycles, high complexity, and the need for highly customized solutions.



**/Workflow Complexity and Stakeholders**

Different payment methods, currencies, banks, and delivery systems increase complexity.

Involvement of finance, sales, and customer success teams. Sales commissions often tied to collections, necessitating their involvement.

Real-time data syncing across different systems and stakeholders, maintaining context for all parties involved.



**/Key Integrations and Data Sources**

CRM and ERP Systems: Integration with CRM (like Salesforce) and ERP (like NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365).

Integration with email, Slack, Microsoft Teams for streamlined communication.

Bank and Payment Gateways: Pulling transaction data from banks and processing payments through gateways.

Using AI to match payments to invoices, handling various formats of remittance advice (emails, PDFs, etc.), and reconciling with ERP.



**/Differentiation and Competitive Landscape**

Offering end-to-end automation for collections, payments, and cash application.

Ease of Implementation: Quick, plug-and-play integrations with existing tech stacks, avoiding long implementation cycles.

Customer Relationship Focus: Emphasizing the importance of customer relationships in collections, not just automation.

Competitors: Tesorio, Versapay, YayPay, High Radius (in some mid-market deals), and other automation-focused providers.

Addressing Manual Processes and Partner Channels

Current way: Mostly companies relying on manual processes and spreadsheets.

Potential partnerships with ERP providers as go-to-market channels, leveraging their ecosystems.



**Help they need in US markets**

1\. Field Marketing in the US

**Team,**

We had a discussion with Pavan from [**CheckRed**][1]**. Here are a few insights. He had very good things about Dayakar and Sriram.**

**Core Insights & Takeaways**

**Industry Landscape: Shift Toward Tech-Enabled Services (MSSP 2.0)**

* Cybersecurity is evolving from pure-product to technology-enabled managed services (MSSP 2.0) — blending automation, AI-driven detection, and revenue-sharing GTM models.

* Players like Rewst Security (US) and Clearwater have demonstrated that combining product + managed service delivery enables fast 0–10M ARR growth and strong exit multiples (10–20×).

The next growth wave isn’t in pure SaaS or consulting, but in platformized managed security services — a sweet spot where BluSapphire can dominate through its MSSP-first architecture.

**  
**

**Go-to-Market Realities: US Expansion via Channel & Ecosystem Plays**

* Direct GTM in the US has high friction; partnerships with ConnectWise, Optiv, and regional MSSPs offer scalable entry with low CAC.

* ConnectWise seen as a “gateway” to 25K+ MSSPs globally — strategic plug-in could give BluSapphire recurring ARR with minimal on-ground cost.

BluSapphire’s channel-led model fits this motion. Focus should be on ConnectWise ecosystem integration and MSSP onboarding vs. direct enterprise chasing.

**  
**

**Product-Market Edge: Multi-Tenant, AI-Automation, and Shared SOC**

* BluSapphire’s multi-tenant SOC architecture and automation can reduce L1/L2 workloads by 80–90%.

* Emerging as a “Shared SOC Infrastructure” provider can position BluSapphire as the AWS for MSSPs — offering outcome-as-a-service (OaaS) rather than headcount-heavy managed services.

Push narrative from SIEM replacement → AI-Driven SOC Fabric that powers MSSPs’ profitability.

**  
**

**Emerging Attack Surfaces: AI Security, SaaS Security, DNS Posture**

* New frontiers are AI Security, SaaS Security Posture (SSPM), and DNS Posture Management (DPM).

* AI-driven attack vectors (e.g., AI-powered malware, data poisoning) are creating demand for new “AI Gateway” and “AI Firewall” layers.

BluSapphire should prioritize early positioning as “AI-Aware SOC” — expanding coverage from traditional infrastructure to AI & data-layer defence.

**Pricing & Positioning: Compete with Splunk via Simplicity + TCO Advantage**

* BluSapphire’s pricing 30–40% lower than Splunk and transparent “what-you-see-is-what-you-get” model gives a clear entry wedge.

* Differentiation lies not just in cost, but in data localization, faster deployment, and zero lock-in – critical for mid-tier enterprises and regulated markets.

Messaging to focus on credibility + simplicity, not “cheapness.” Lead with outcomes (“Reduce SOC cost by 40%, scale detections by 2×”).

**Strategic**

**  
**

**Next Steps**

**Ecosystem Entry – ConnectWise Partnership**

* Begin exploratory call with ConnectWise ecosystem lead to scope MSSP onboarding and integration path.

* Build joint GTM model – revenue share structure + pilot MSSP.

**  
**

**Channel Activation**

* Identify 3–5 strong MSSPs (India, GCC, and US) to run “Shared SOC” pilots under revenue-sharing model.

* Offer flexible onboarding, zero entry cost, and revenue uplift framework (20–40% margin boost).

**US Market Setup**

* Hire or partner with a channel-focused US GTM leader/advisor (suggested by Pavan) to anchor BD and partnership development.

* Establish presence through regional MSSP events (Black Hat, MSSP Alert Live, SecureWorld) rather than generic cybersecurity expos.

**  
**

**Product Evolution**

* Prioritize AI-driven correlation, DNS posture analytics, and AI Gateway integration in roadmap.

* Build “Outcome-as-a-Service” module for MSSPs — combining analytics, orchestration, and automation in one bundle.

**Positioning & Narrative Refresh**

* Shift BluSapphire’s story from “NextGen SIEM” to “AI-Driven SOC Platform powering MSSPs.”

* Develop 1-pager comparing BluSapphire vs. Splunk / Chronicle on TCO, automation depth, and MSSP fit. - they have it

**  
**

**Expected Outcomes**

* 2–3 new MSSP partnerships through ConnectWise ecosystem.

* 1 active pilot in the US with revenue-share model.

* Strengthened AI-security narrative with DNS/AI Gateway module prototype.

* Revised US GTM strategy anchored by advisor-led channel motion.

* Clear differentiation story leading to stronger valuation positioning for next raise.

1\. Phani Neti highlighted that Intelysis operates in a crowded space with many competitors like SAP, Siemens etc. but sees an opportunity for them to be the \"Zoho for manufacturing/productivity\" focused on the Indian market.



2\. Shyam Penumaka pointed out key challenges around complex revenue structure, marketplace offerings, geographical focus on India/SE Asia, exit options and IC approval.



NEXT STEPS



1\. Raghav Mishra to create list of questions on financial data, revenue structure, customer information etc. and circulate to Shyam and Phani.

2\. Schedule follow up call with Intelysis with Google also present to discuss additional findings.

3\. Research Wipro as potential customer and acquisition source.



TOPICS DISCUSSED



1\. Company Overview



\- Intelysis provides manufacturing execution system (MES) and supply chain management software focused on the manufacturing vertical.

\- They have over 40 customers across automotive, engineering, electronics, FMCG industries etc.



2\. Competitor Analysis



\- Main competitors are SAP, Siemens, Oracle etc. but Intelysis is cost competitive and faster to deploy for manufacturing units.

\- Intelysis has positioned themselves to have comparable features as SAP at lower cost according to their deck.



3\. Product Offerings



\- Main product is the manufacturing execution system (MES) and supply chain module along with Zestlink data analytics platform and Zestfloor integrated portal.

\- Provide modules for inventory management, production planning, quality management, warehouse management etc.



4\. Business Model



\- Currently follow a perpetual license model with annual maintenance contracts.

\- Have a complex revenue structure with one time license fees, annual maintenance fees as recurring component.

\- Also offer consulting/services for SAP implementations.



5\. Revenue Structure



\- Clarification needed on definitive recurring revenue vs one time license sales.

\- ARR is currently INR 1.7 million but details needed to break it down into licensing, maintenance, services etc.



6\. Market Opportunity



\- India manufacturing sector expected to grow rapidly so huge potential based on government push.

\- Can focus on Indian manufacturing units and expand to south-east Asia but global expansion requires more assessment.



7\. Customer Base



\- Have leading Indian manufacturing companies like Amara Raja, Dixon, Anchor, Panasonic etc. as clients currently.

\- Opportunity for upsell into more factories/product modules within same customer accounts.



8\. Partner Ecosystem



\- Partners like Panasonic, MotherSon indicate possible exit via acquisition from strategics in manufacturing space itself.

\- Also exploring working with ENY consulting.



9\. Meeting Preparation



\- Raghav Mishra was unprepared for the meeting without reviewing deck or recording prior to call.

\- Need to send prep questions to Intelysis beforehand for next meeting.
